newsitem.title: KENYA: RALLYING-SAINZ BIDS TO MAINTAIN CHAMPIONSHIP LEAD.
newsitem.headline: RALLYING-SAINZ BIDS TO MAINTAIN CHAMPIONSHIP LEAD.

text.p: Carlos Sainz of Spain heads into this weekend's Safari Rally in Kenya as a firm contender for victory if he can maintain the reliability that has brought him the lead in this year's World Rally Championship.
The Kenya-based event, the third round of the championship and historically the longest, fastest and toughest rally on the calendar, has a new, shorter format this year.

But none of the competing teams are under the illusion that it will be any easier than in the past. On two occasions only seven cars have crossed the finish line -- and the teams have all been working hard in the build-up to this year's event hoping that statistic will not be repeated.

"We have already spent a lot of time in Africa preparing for this rally," said Sainz, who won the event in 1992. "We are already in much better shape than we were last year because we have learned a lot about the Escort and improved its durability."
The Kenyan Rally, a three-day event centred around Nairobi, is unique in that all its competitive stages take place on open public roads.

This has forced teams to use helicopters to fly ahead of the cars and warn them of any hazards on the road, including vehicles and wild animals. The Mitsubishi team are so concerned about the dangers that they have hired a doctor for each of their helicopters.

"The important thing here is to get to the finish. That will be our main objective. With our strategy of driving fast enough to keep in touch, yet carefully enough to avoid problems, we will be looking for a possible top three finish," said Sainz.

The Spaniard's German team mate, Armin Schwarz, also believes that reliability will be a key factor to the outcome, thanks to new service rules that limit the amount of outside assistance each crew can receive.
"I am sure some of my rivals will start really fast and think the car is strong enough to treat the Safari like a short European event," he explained.
"I am not so worried about the rough places where you must go at walking speed -- everybody can judge those -- but the problem comes on the high-speed stretches.
"If you miss just one dried-up river crossing, you can damage the car so badly that your rally can be over. The car that holds together will win this rally."
Kenneth Eriksson of Finland hopes to repeat his victory of last year. His chances will be boosted by the addition of Briton Richard Burns to his Mitsubishi team.

The first leg of the rally starts on Saturday and its four competitive stages take the teams to the south of Nairobi, before Sunday's five stages take them north of the Kenyan capital. The final leg on Monday follows the same route as the first day with an afternoon finish in Nairobi.
